text: Fault tree analysis is a deductive, top-down technique: reasoning proceeds from a general postulated failure of the system toward the specific lower-level faults that can bring it about. The analyst assumes the undesired system state has occurred and works backward to assemble, in a systematic and logical way, the chains of more basic faults that contribute to it. This contrasts with inductive (bottom-up) methods, which start from an assumed component fault or initiating event and trace its effects upward to the system. Deduction answers how a given failed state can arise; induction answers what states are possible. Because it is deductive, a fault tree is a structured model of the necessary and sufficient relationships among events that culminate in the top event, not a catalog of effects accumulated from individual part failures.

topic: Steps of a fault tree analysis
text: A fault tree analysis proceeds through an ordered set of steps. First, identify the objective the analysis must serve, phrased as a failure of the system under study. Second, define the top event that represents that failure. Third, define the scope, fixing which failures and contributors are included and which are excluded. Fourth, define the resolution, the level of detail to which causes will be developed. Fifth, set ground rules and naming conventions. Sixth, construct the tree. Seventh, evaluate it qualitatively and quantitatively. Eighth, interpret and present the results. The first five steps frame the problem; scope, resolution, and ground rules can be developed concurrently and are often revised during construction and evaluation. Emphasis belongs on interpretation, not mere documentation, so that findings translate into actionable implications for the original objective.

The top event governs the entire analysis; if it is defined incorrectly, the whole fault tree and any decisions drawn from it will be wrong. Define the top event in terms of the specific criteria that constitute its occurrence. For a system failure, first state the system success criteria, then define failure as the negation of those criteria. Confirm that the chosen top event is consistent with the analysis objective and the actual problem to be solved; analysts have frequently picked a plausible-sounding top event that did not match the decision maker's intent. When uncertain, formulate several candidate top events and assess the applicability of each before committing. The initial state of the system should be fixed as part of the top-event definition or the scope. A separate top event may be needed for each distinct objective or each mission phase.

topic: Scope and boundaries of the analysis
text: Define the boundaries of the analysis before construction begins and document them; if they shift during construction, record the changes. Scope fixes what is inside the analysis (the contributors and events whose relationship to the top event will be developed) and what is outside (contributors that will not be developed). It also fixes the design version, the time period, the operating modes, and the boundary conditions, including component initial states and assumed inputs to the system. A fault tree is a snapshot of the system at a given time, in a given configuration, under a given boundary. Interfaces such as power, cooling, or supply sources sit at the boundary: if they are excluded, their assumed states must still be specified so the inputs to the analyzed components are defined. Good practice is to show interfaces and their assumed states explicitly, which documents the boundary and lets external models be attached later.

Resolution is the level of detail to which the causes of the top event are developed. A functional system failure is generally resolved down to the major components, such as valves, pumps, and control modules. A phenomenological top event is resolved to the level at which its causes are meaningfully modeled. The guiding aim is to develop the tree to a depth where adequate failure-probability data exist and where further subdivision no longer changes the risk discrimination. Deeper resolution becomes necessary when decisions hinge on subcomponents or support systems, or when an event cannot be shown independent of others, such as shared actuation signals or shared power. Developing below the level where data exist, or below the level where distinctions matter, is usually unnecessary and counterproductive.

Before constructing a fault tree, establish ground rules that govern how events and gates are named and how particular kinds of failures are to be modeled. A clear, agreed naming scheme is essential to an understandable tree and to correct evaluation. Modeling ground rules promote consistency, which matters especially when several analysts build different trees that must be compared or combined. Such rules can specify how component failures, human errors, and common-cause failures are represented. Settling these conventions up front, and putting procedures in place to avoid accidentally giving one event two different names, prevents errors that are costly to fix later: renaming events in an already-built tree is difficult and error-prone.

The core construction paradigm is to think small, or more precisely to think myopically. For each event under analysis, identify only the necessary and sufficient immediate events, the most closely related causes that directly produce it. Do not jump ahead to the basic or root causes. Instead, take one small step backward at a time, naming the immediate causes, then treat each of those as a new event and repeat. This stepwise backward tracing guarantees that no intermediate relationship or contributing event is skipped, and it reveals the precise logic that is necessary and sufficient for the event. The process terminates when the backward stepping reaches the basic causes that define the chosen resolution of the analysis.

The immediate-cause concept, also called the Think Small rule, directs the analyst to find the immediate, necessary, and sufficient causes of each event rather than its underlying basic causes. After defining the system boundary and selecting a failure mode as the top event, determine that event's immediate causes, then treat each as a sub-top event and find its immediate causes in turn. With each step the analyst's viewpoint shifts from failure mechanism to failure mode and the resolution grows finer, continuing until the limit of resolution, the basic component faults, is reached. Taking only one step at a time is what assures completeness: skipping ahead can silently omit a valid intermediate cause, for example a path where an input is present but the component still fails to produce its output.

A distinction is drawn between failures and the broader notion of faults. A failure is a basic abnormal occurrence: a component does not perform as required when conditions call for it. A fault is a higher-order, more general event: the component may operate exactly as built but at the wrong time or in response to an improper command from elsewhere, putting the larger system into an undesirable state. Thus all failures are faults, but not all faults are failures. Properly specifying a fault requires stating both what the undesired state is and when it occurs; both the what and the when belong in the event description entered into the tree. As a working convention during construction, an event that is developed further is termed a fault, while a basic input that is not developed further is termed a failure.

System, subsystem, and component are relative designations chosen for convenience to give the problem a hierarchy and boundaries; a key strength of fault tree analysis is that elements are viewed by function rather than by artificial structural boundaries. Three linked ideas organize the causal chain. A failure effect is why a failure matters, its consequence on the system. A failure mode is the specific manner in which a failure presents. A failure mechanism is how a given mode comes about. Mechanisms produce modes, and modes produce effects. The same event changes label with the observer's level: what is a mechanism at one level is a mode at the next level down and an effect at the level below that. Moving down the tree, the analyst continually re-views each event from mechanism to mode while approaching finer resolution.

Fault tree analysis is powerful precisely because it looks past nominal system boundaries and examines the role each subsystem or component plays in the overall design. While stepping down the tree, the analyst must watch for cases in which faults originating in other systems can cause a component to fail, and must investigate those external faults rather than assume the component is isolated. Causes that lie beneath one analyst's chosen limit of resolution, such as quality-control, manufacturing, or environmental effects on a component, may nevertheless be dominant contributors to overall system failure and should not be dismissed merely because they fall below the system designer's normal level of interest.

Evaluating a fault tree yields cut sets, also called failure sets. A cut set is a collection of basic events whose simultaneous occurrence produces the top event, directly linking the bottom-level events to the top. A minimal cut set is a smallest such collection: if any of its events does not occur, that combination no longer causes the top event. A tree has a finite number of unique minimal cut sets, and together they enumerate every distinct way the top event can happen in terms of basic events. Cut sets are often sorted by order, the number of events they contain, to reveal how many simultaneous failures are required. Path sets are the logical complement, drawn from the success tree: a path set is a set of events whose joint non-occurrence guarantees the top event does not occur, and a minimal path set is a smallest such set, enumerating the unique ways to assure success.

topic: Success space and the success tree
text: Analysis may be carried out equivalently in failure space or in success space. The fault tree works in failure space, modeling combinations of faults that produce the undesired event. Its logical complement is the success tree, which models the conditions that guarantee the undesired event does not occur; the minimal path sets of the success tree are the complements of the minimal cut sets of the fault tree. The two formulations describe the same system and yield consistent results. In many cases the failure-space approach is the less laborious of the two, which is why fault trees remain the primary working tool, but recognizing the equivalence lets the analyst cross-check a result or reason about guaranteed-success conditions when that perspective is more convenient.

Two gates underlie all fault tree logic. An OR gate produces its output fault when at least one of its input faults occurs; its inputs are restatements of the output, each made more specific as to cause or scenario, so causes do not feed an OR gate directly. An AND gate produces its output fault only when all of its input faults occur; here the inputs collectively represent the cause of the output, so causes may input an AND gate directly. Other gates are special cases of these two. Because OR inputs are refinements of the output while AND inputs are joint causes, the choice between them must reflect the real necessary-and-sufficient logic of the system, never mere convenience of drawing.

When events feeding an AND gate are not independent, the dependency must be written into the event definitions wherever it affects the system logic. Dependencies typically arise when one failure changes the system, for example by switching in a standby unit or altering operating modes and stress levels in a way that changes how the remaining fault can occur. In such cases a later input should be defined as that fault given the prior fault has occurred, and the subtree describing the mechanisms of the conditioned event will differ from the subtree for the unconditioned event. A priority-form AND gate can make ordered dependence explicit. With multiple dependent inputs, each given condition must incorporate all the preceding events.

Several specialized gates refine the two basic types. An INHIBIT gate is a special AND gate in which a single input produces the output only when a stated qualifying or enabling condition holds; the condition is recorded in a conditioning event drawn beside the gate. A PRIORITY AND gate is an AND gate that fires only when its inputs occur in a specified order, again noted in an attached conditioning event. An EXCLUSIVE OR gate is an OR gate that fires when one input occurs but not when both do; in most modeling the quantitative difference from an ordinary OR is negligible and can be deferred to quantification. A COMBINATION gate fires when a specified number of its inputs occur, providing a convenient way to express threshold logic without enumerating every qualifying combination.

Basic events are events not developed further; each needs a probability if the tree is to be quantified. A circle denotes a primary basic event, a basic initiating fault that requires no further development because the chosen limit of resolution has been reached. A diamond denotes an undeveloped event, a fault left undeveloped either because it is of insufficient consequence or because the information needed to develop it is unavailable. An ellipse denotes a conditioning event, recording a condition or restriction attached to a gate, used chiefly with INHIBIT and PRIORITY AND gates. A house denotes an event normally expected to occur, such as an anticipated change of phase; a house event is not itself a fault. Transfer symbols link a portion of the tree developed elsewhere to its attachment point, avoiding duplication and letting a large tree be split for clarity.

Component faults fall into three useful categories. A primary fault is a fault occurring within the environment for which the component was qualified, such as a component breaking under conditions it was designed to withstand. A secondary fault occurs in an environment beyond what the component was qualified for, that is, under conditions exceeding its design, including damage from external stresses or loss of environmental control. Primary and secondary faults are generally component failures and are often called primary and secondary failures. A command fault involves the component operating properly but at the wrong time or place, typically due to an improper or mistimed signal, or failing to operate because a control signal or control power was lost. These categories serve as a checklist; analysts who take shortcuts sometimes omit secondary or command faults, leaving the tree incomplete.

It is useful to separate components into passive and active types. A passive component contributes in a largely static way, transmitting energy, loads, or a signal from one place to another, or serving as the medium by which one active component's output becomes another's input; its failure means loss of that transmission. An active component contributes dynamically, modifying system behavior and generally requiring an input or trigger to produce its output, so it acts as a transfer function; its failure can mean no output or an incorrect output. These definitions apply to the component's primary function. The distinction matters for both modeling and quantification, since active and passive components typically differ substantially in failure rate.

topic: Ground Rule I: writing fault statements
text: Ground Rule I governs how event boxes are filled in: write each entry as a fault, stating precisely what the fault is and the conditions under which it occurs, and never mix successes with faults. Every fault statement should carry two parts. The what-condition describes the relevant failed or operating state of the component. The when-condition describes the state of the system, relative to that component, that makes that component state a fault. Verbose statements are acceptable and often necessary; do not shorten the description to fit a drawn box or abbreviate the underlying idea. Abbreviating words is fine, but the full meaning of each event must be preserved so the logic remains unambiguous.

topic: Ground Rule II: component vs system fault
text: After writing a fault statement, ask whether it is a state-of-component fault or a state-of-system fault; this is Ground Rule II. If the fault is a component failure localized to a single component, classify it as state-of-component. If it is not localized to one component, and instead involves a system-level condition or the occurrence of multiple faults, classify it as state-of-system. The classification dictates the next structure. A state-of-component fault is developed by placing an OR gate beneath it and seeking primary, secondary, and command contributions, or it is left as a primary event. A state-of-system fault is developed by finding the minimum necessary and sufficient immediate causes, which may call for an AND, OR, or INHIBIT gate, or possibly no gate at all. As a guide, when the driving energy originates outside the component, the fault is usually state-of-system.

The No Miracles rule governs how the normal behavior of components is treated while tracing a fault sequence. If the normal functioning of a component would help propagate a fault sequence, assume the component functions normally and let the sequence pass; do not rely on a fortuitous, unexpected failure to block it. Conversely, if the normal functioning of a component would block a fault sequence, then that normal function must itself be defeated by faults for the sequence to continue upward, and the model must represent the faults required to defeat it. Put differently, wherever the real system imposes an AND condition, the tree must capture it rather than wish it away.

Two procedural rules guard against unmethodical shortcutting. The Complete-the-Gate rule requires that all inputs to a gate be fully defined before any one of them is developed further; the tree is built level by level, each level finished before the next is begun. The No Gate-to-Gate rule requires that every gate input be a properly defined fault event, so gates are never wired directly to other gates. A gate-to-gate connection signals sloppy analysis and often reveals that the analyst does not yet fully understand the system. Both rules reflect the underlying truth that a fault tree succeeds only when the analyst has a clear and complete understanding of the system being modeled.

How a fault is modeled follows directly from its classification. A state-of-component fault is always represented either as a primary event or as an OR gate; for instance a component's functional failure may be an OR of an internal failure of the component and a failure of the signal commanding it. A state-of-system fault is represented with whichever gate captures the real logic among the contributing components. For a redundancy where every unit must fail to cause the system fault, an OR over the upstream causes may apply; where any one unit failing is sufficient, an AND of the unit failures applies. The analyst selects the gate by working out the necessary and sufficient immediate causes, not by habit.

The depth to which a fault tree is built determines how meaningful its results are, and erring toward excessive depth is more common and more damaging than insufficient depth. Building too deep wastes effort and injects extra uncertainty and obscurity, because data are sparse or absent at very fine levels and because decomposing an entity into many sub-parts scatters it across the results and obscures its identity. The governing principle: develop the tree only to the depth needed to identify functional dependencies and relationships among events, and to a depth consistent with the available data and the analysis objective. A system failure is usually developed to the major-component or major-contributor level. Depth for its own sake is misguided; the necessary depth is whatever is required to expose dependencies, no more.

Fault tree depth must be driven by the system architecture supplied to the analyst, not invented. Stop developing a branch at the level the architecture actually resolves: the major components, contributors, and support interfaces that the described system exposes. Do not introduce structure, sub-parts, or basic events that the given architecture does not support, since decomposing past that level fragments recognizable entities and produces basic events for which no data and no decision relevance exist. Show the support interfaces, such as power and cooling supplies, because these are what reveal hardwired and functional dependencies among components. The right stopping point is the level where dependencies are exposed and where credible data attach; descending below what the architecture and data justify only inflates uncertainty without improving the model.

topic: Why FMEAs cannot be combined into a tree
text: Failure modes and effects analyses cannot be patched together to form a fault tree, and attempting it is bad practice that yields an erroneous model. An FMEA is built bottom-up, linking selected initiating causes to their consequences, and because those consequences resemble events in a tree it can seem they could be stitched into a top or intermediate event. They cannot. A fault tree is a top-down structure of the immediate, necessary, and sufficient relationships among events, within which basic events are identified exhaustively and consistently. An FMEA selects its initiating causes without a defining logic structure and does not show the relationships among causes, so it cannot guarantee the comprehensiveness or consistency a tree provides, nor reveal where causes are redundant or absorbed by others. An FMEA can usefully check a constructed tree or help decide whether and how deeply to build one, but it cannot substitute for deductive construction.

The definition of the top event determines the structure of the entire tree, and the same physical system can produce very different trees depending on which failure is chosen as the top event. A loss-of-function top event, such as no flow or no signal reaching a destination, typically resolves into an OR of several single failures, because any one of several blockages can interrupt the function. An inadvertent-function top event, such as undesired flow or signal where none should occur, typically resolves into an AND of multiple failures, because every element in the path must wrongly pass for the unwanted output to reach the end. This parallelism, with AND gates replacing OR gates between the two formulations, recurs generally, and the applicable component failure modes differ between the two, so they would require different data.

Common-cause failures are two or more component failures arising from a single shared cause at the same time or within a short interval. The relevant common causes are implicit dependencies not already captured by explicitly modeled functional dependencies; they include shared design or material deficiencies, common installation or maintenance errors, and shared harsh environments. Because a single such cause can disable an entire redundant set, neglecting it can grossly underestimate the top-event probability, so common-cause contributions must be modeled explicitly. The key is to identify which components are susceptible and represent the shared cause as a separate contributor, for example as an additional event combined with the independent-failure logic of a redundant group. A cause already modeled explicitly is not also treated as common-cause, but other shared causes still must be added.

Common-cause failures are generally most important for redundant, identical, active components, and become more dominant as the number of redundant units grows. A sound rule of thumb is to include a common-cause contribution for any redundancy of identical active components, and to add one for identical redundant passive or electrical components when they are judged potentially susceptible; when in doubt, include it. The contribution can be modeled at the component level, or at the train or subsystem level if those units are identical and suitable common-cause data exist at that level; if there is any doubt, model it at the basic-component level. After modeling, sensitivity studies can reveal how strongly the top-event probability depends on the common-cause probability, and contributors that prove influential can then be analyzed in more detail.

Human errors can be important contributors and should be represented in a fault tree to give a realistic failure picture. The decision is whether to model an error explicitly or fold it into an equipment probability. A test or maintenance error need not be modeled explicitly if the resulting equipment failure is already in the tree, provided that equipment's probability then includes the human contribution; but it should be modeled explicitly when it produces a misconfiguration rather than a failure, since misconfigurations differ in nature and recovery, and always when one error can disable two or more components. An error that can affect multiple sites is modeled with a single shared identifier so its common impact is captured. When in doubt, model the error explicitly. Human errors are represented as basic events causing an equipment failure or misconfiguration.

topic: Types of human error and commission
text: Several categories of human error may warrant modeling: test and maintenance errors, errors that cause initiating events, procedural errors during a response, errors of omission, and detection or recovery errors. Errors causing initiating events are usually folded into initiating-event frequencies and modeled explicitly only when not already included there or when one action causes multiple impacts, such as initiating an event while also disabling a mitigating component. Procedural and omission errors, like failing to act or to change a component's state, are modeled as basic events attributing an equipment effect to human error. Detection and recovery errors may be modeled to show their contribution or otherwise absorbed into equipment probabilities. Errors of commission, unforeseen inappropriate actions, are generally not modeled, because bounding their scope and assigning probabilities is impractical. How each type will be handled should be decided when scope and approach are defined.

When systems exchange signals in a feedback arrangement, a naive fault tree can form a logical loop, for instance by listing one system's failure as a cause of a second system's failure while also listing the second as a cause of the first, which absurdly makes a system cause its own failure. To prevent this, when developing the branch where one system fails because of a failed signal from another, include only the internal failures of the system that originates that signal; do not trace failures arising from the feedback itself. Applying this rule, that only internal failures of the originating system are considered, to any number of interacting systems cuts the loops so none appear in the resulting tree. The internal failures developed may differ between the trees for the different systems.

A phenomenological sequence consists of an initiating event followed by pivotal events leading to an undesired outcome, and is usually modeled with an event sequence diagram or event tree, though a fault tree can be used when desired. When it is, the final undesired outcome becomes the top event, and the sequence is typically represented by an AND gate combining the events. Because later events depend on earlier ones, their conditional nature must be made explicit in the event descriptions, each stating the given conditions under which it occurs, so the proper order is preserved and the probabilities assigned are conditional on the preceding events. If explicit ordering must be enforced, replace the AND gate with a PRIORITY AND gate to guarantee the physical sequence is retained.

Naming matters because correct cut sets and probabilities depend on consistent identifiers when a gate or basic event appears more than once. If one identical component failure is given two different names, an AND gate would misread a single failure as two failures, and under an OR gate the event would be double counted. Identifiers should be concise and descriptive and fit any character limits the software imposes. A common form for a component failure combines component type, a unique component identifier, and the failure mode; a system or element identifier can be prepended when several systems are modeled. Intermediate events can follow similar conventions. Above all, adopt an agreed naming scheme before construction and use procedures to prevent giving one event two names, since renaming a finished tree is difficult and error-prone.

Several ground rules narrow a tree's scope without harming results, but each must be checked for applicability to the problem at hand. Model to the highest level for which data exist and at which there are no shared hardware interfaces with other contributors, generally the major-component level; deeper modeling wastes effort and inflates uncertainty, following the maxim that too much detail brings too much uncertainty. Wiring and piping faults between components are generally omitted because their probabilities are low, unless no higher contributors exist, the objective requires them, or they can be affected by other failures such as fire or aging. Out-of-design conditions are generally not modeled and require justification if included. Stop developing an AND gate of high order when lower-order combinations already exist and no shared interfaces link its inputs, and stop developing an OR-gate input shown to have far lower probability than other inputs, leaving such events undeveloped.

Because a tree's quantitative output is an intangible probability, validation is indirect but important. Obtain the minimal cut sets and confirm that the smallest-order ones are genuine failure paths to the top event, checking against the system schematic. Check that failures and events recorded in operating history actually appear in the tree, testing scope and completeness. Obtain the success paths and validate that the smallest are real success paths. If validating the top event directly is too hard, validate the cut sets and success paths of intermediate faults instead. Finally, sanity-check probabilities: low-order cut sets and those with active-component failures should rank highest, modeled common-cause and human-error contributions should appear prominent, and intermediate and top-event probabilities should be reasonable against past experience. Extremely small top-event probabilities are usually fictitious and indicate that more likely failure paths were missed.
